prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms enables frequency measurement at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: the optical lattice clock alone, credited to Katori and Ye. After reading all eight first-round files, the scientific case looks the same from every angle on the committee. The magic-wavelength condition cancels the trapping light shift, which is what allows very many neutral atoms to be interrogated at once; that is a distinct physical idea and not a refinement of single-ion control. It has been reproduced by independent laboratories at uncertainties near 1e-18, and it has concrete consequences in clock comparisons, relativistic geodesy, tests of constants and dark-sector couplings, and the preparation of a new definition of the second. Six members now prefer it and two more list it as an alternative, and I note that this convergence came from members whose opening favourites were different (Higgs, circuit QED, CMB), who moved because of the attribution and maturity arguments rather than because of a count. The two-name credit follows the chain of the work: concept and first realisation with Katori, systematic accuracy and many-body clock physics with Ye. The chair asked whether a citation can cover the invention without trespassing on the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I think it can, by naming the lattice clock and its defining mechanism, magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, and by saying nothing about optical clocks or precision spectroscopy in general.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize remains the strongest reservation, because the lattice clock depends on both technologies, and a committee could reasonably decide that the territory has been served. I judge the overlap as real but not decisive, because the many-atom lattice concept is what is being credited. Two names also cannot capture Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups, so the prize is a judgement on credit and not a partition of it, and my own view of the Katori and Ye split rests on general knowledge, not on verified records. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the downstream payoff is still prospective. I do not think this outweighs demonstrated impact, but I cannot rule out that a committee more cautious than I am would wait. Broad support is also not a scientific argument by itself, and I have tried not to use it as one.

responses.point: Preferred B019 and, in answer to my round-1 note, argued that the citation can be worded around the Z2 prediction and the first observation of the quantum spin Hall state, with the symmetry-class insight belonging to Kane and Mele even though the HgTe proposal of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang sharpened the material choice.
responses.response: Your wording argument is the best available answer to the attribution problem, and I accept that Kane and Mele's classification is the conceptual core. I do not think it fully removes the difficulty, though. A citation naming the first observation in HgTe will invite the question of why the proposal that identified HgTe is outside it, and the 2016 prize on topological phases lies close enough that the novelty argument must be made explicitly. Neither point makes B019 weak. They make it a prize that has to be defended against a visible objection, where the clock does not, so I keep it as my principal alternative and not my preferred part. I do not want it paired with B048, since three laureates would force a split of the clock credit that I do not think is warranted.

responses.point: Preferred B028 (spherical-aberration correction) but said she would regard B048 as a defensible outcome, and asked in her reply to me for a tightly drafted citation separating the lattice concept from general precision spectroscopy.
responses.response: I take your request for a tight citation seriously, and the revised wording above is meant to answer it: it names the lattice clock and its mechanism, magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, and does not refer to optical clocks in general. I also accept that B028 is a clear invention with a more settled three-name credit than most of the shortlist, and I would not call it an inferior part. My remaining difference is about where the discovery sits. Its impact is greatest in materials science and chemistry, and the Krivanek and STEM question you raise yourself means the TEM-only trio would be deciding a priority matter. I would not oppose it, but I place it below the clock, and I read your own statement that B048 would be a defensible outcome as agreement that the two cases can be settled in favour of the clock without injustice.

responses.point: Raised trapped-ion quantum logic (B003) as a possible second part alongside B048, and noted that the question of a second part is open.
responses.response: I considered this seriously and still decline it. A two-part prize needs at most three people in total, so adding B003 means either splitting the clock credit to one name or dropping Cirac, Zoller or Blatt, and both outcomes damage a case that is currently clean. B003 also has the overlap with the 2012 prize and the experimental-priority question that Johansson and Lindroth raised, with Monroe and other ion groups outside Blatt. I keep B003 as an alternative for a later year or as a fallback if the committee disagrees on B048, but I would not combine it with the clock. A single-achievement, two-laureate prize is the preferable outcome.

responses.point: Argued that the citation should name the optical lattice clock with magic-wavelength trapping and not optical clocks in general, and that the demonstrated impact outweighs the timing argument about the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with the citation point and have adopted it. On timing, my view is close to yours but more guarded: I think the demonstrated impact on clock comparison and geodesy justifies acting now, but I cannot judge from this record how close the redefinition of the second is, and I would be more comfortable if you, who work closer to precision atomic physics than I do, confirmed that the 1e-18 comparisons are reproduced across laboratories as the files say. If that holds, I do not think waiting would strengthen the case; if the redefinition were to stall, waiting would also not weaken it.

responses.point: Moved from the Higgs discovery to B048 and said that the three-person limit fits the lattice clock without forcing arbitrary exclusions, while noting the Higgs remains the most consequential outstanding experimental result.
responses.response: I agree that the clock's credit fits the statutory limit better than any ATLAS and CMS selection does, and I think your own attribution test is correct. I would add that your point about the Higgs being overdue is a statement about importance, not about who should be named, and the committee should keep the two apart. If the committee later chooses to honour the experiments, a citation built on the detector leadership will be needed, and I would want to hear the case then. For this vote I do not see it displacing the lattice clock, and your chair flags on B033 and B054 do not affect my preference.

responses.point: Argued that the lattice clock is a discovery-and-invention in which nature supplied the magic-wavelength condition, and that it is the one case where support does not rest on one member's field.
responses.response: I agree that the support does not depend on a single field, and I find your framing of nature supplying the magic-wavelength condition a useful way to answer the charge that this is only engineering. The condition is a property of the atomic structure that was identified and then exploited, which is a discovery element as well as an invention. I would not go as far as to treat spread of support as a merit argument, and I am glad you also list it as an uncertainty. Where we differ slightly is on B033, which you keep as an alternative: I rank B019 and B003 above it because I find the IceCube credit to Halzen and Karle less complete.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize to warrant a separate award.

Whether the credit to Katori and Ye alone is fair given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups, and which priority details are verified and which are recollection; my own are general knowledge.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes waiting preferable, which I cannot resolve from the record.
Whether a second part is possible without splitting the clock credit; I still see no natural fit within three laureates.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye or the other shortlisted candidates, and my research on turbulent aerosols, random matrices and neural networks is distant from all shortlisted topics. I note the proximity flags raised by Johansson, Kroll, Olsson and the chair, and none of them touches my preferred configuration.
